title: Johnson & Johnson Wins FDA Nod for Ottava Surgical Robot
excerpt: The authorisation clears J&J to challenge Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci system in the soft-tissue robotic surgery market with a table-integrated design that takes up half the space.
body:
• Johnson & Johnson's Ottava robotic system has received FDA approval for various upper-abdomen surgeries.
  • Ottava requires 30-50% less space than traditional surgical robots, enhancing operating room efficiency.
  • The system aims to challenge Intuitive Surgical's established da Vinci platform in the robotic surgery market.
  • J&J plans to launch Ottava in the U.S. while pursuing approvals in additional international markets.
Key Takeaways
  • J&J's Ottava robotic system is FDA-approved for various upper-abdomen surgeries.
  • Ottava occupies 30-50% less space than traditional surgical robots.
  • The system aims to compete with Intuitive Surgical's long-dominant da Vinci platform.
  • J&J plans a U.S. launch while seeking approvals in other markets.
  • The launch comes as J&J's medtech division seeks new growth opportunities.
Ottava's Surgical Capabilities
›Approved for multiple upper-abdomen procedures.
›Procedures include gastric bypass, gallbladder removal, and hernia repair.
›Supported by FORTE clinical study with 30 patients.
›All procedures completed robotically without conversion.

Johnson & Johnson said on Wednesday that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted marketing authorisation for its Ottava robotic surgical system, clearing the healthcare giant to compete in the fast-growing soft-tissue robotic surgery market currently dominated by Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci platform.

The approval marks the culmination of a development effort that began in 2020 and was delayed by roughly two years due to multiple setbacks, making it one of the most closely watched product launches in the medtech industry.

A New Challenger in the Operating Room

The Ottava system received authorisation via the FDA's de novo classification pathway for use in multiple general surgery procedures in the upper abdomen, including gastric bypass, gastrectomy, gallbladder removal, gastric sleeve surgery, appendectomy and hiatal hernia repair.

The authorisation was supported by data from J&J's FORTE clinical study, in which a 30-patient cohort undergoing Roux-en-Y gastric bypass procedures met primary safety and performance endpoints through 30 days post-procedure. All procedures were completed robotically without conversion to a non-robotic approach, according to results presented at the 2026 American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery annual meeting.

“We have taken learnings from Johnson & Johnson's 140 years in surgery and the experiences robotic surgeons and hospitals have had over the past 20 years to design a soft tissue robotic system built for the future of surgery.”

— Hani Abouhalka, Company Group Chair, Surgery, MedTech, J&J

Design That Changes the Equation

Unlike conventional surgical robots that use boom-and-cart-mounted arms wheeled into the operating room, Ottava's robotic arms are integrated directly into the operating table. J&J said this design allows the system to occupy 30 to 50 percent less space than competing platforms, potentially enabling robotic surgery in operating rooms that could not previously accommodate such equipment.

The space advantage is not trivial. Many hospitals, particularly smaller facilities and those in emerging markets, have been unable to adopt robotic surgery due to the physical footprint requirements of existing systems. J&J is positioning Ottava as a solution to expand the addressable market well beyond the large academic medical centres that have traditionally been early adopters.

Space-Saving Design Advantage
›Ottava's arms integrated into the operating table.
›Occupies 30-50% less space than conventional systems.
›Enables robotic surgery in smaller hospitals.
›Addresses market limitations for emerging facilities.

Challenging the Da Vinci Dynasty

Intuitive Surgical has dominated the soft-tissue robotic surgery market since the da Vinci system received FDA clearance in 2000. Medtronic's Hugo robotic system, which received its first FDA authorisation for urologic procedures in December 2025, is the other major competitor.

J&J's entry is significant because of the company's existing scale in surgery. As one of the world's largest medical device makers, J&J has deep relationships with hospitals and a vast portfolio of surgical instruments that could be integrated with the Ottava platform.

What Lies Ahead

Market Dynamics: A New Challenger
Intuitive Surgical (da Vinci)
Dominant since 2000
Medtronic (Hugo)
FDA clearance in 2025
Johnson & Johnson (Ottava)
FDA approved in 2023

J&J said it would begin a U.S. commercial launch with select customers while working to expand the system into additional indications and regulatory markets. The company also received FDA approval in late 2025 for an investigational device exemption to study Ottava in inguinal hernia procedures, one of the most commonly performed surgeries in the United States.

The approval comes at a delicate moment for J&J's medtech division. Last week, the unit missed quarterly sales estimates after demand for its Impella heart pumps declined following a UK study that raised questions about their use during certain high-risk coronary procedures. The Ottava launch offers a new growth vector at a time the company needs one.
